intro: Game suggestions from two rounds: the first five came from the market research; the second five came out of the Idea lab, where 80 ideas were generated, scored by two judges and attacked by two critics. Everything is ranked for your model by default: one person building with AI, web-first, marketed on TikTok and YouTube.
caveat: No dataset can guarantee a hit, and most games, web or Steam, earn very little. Each suggestion is a bet backed by specific signals, with gates that tell you early whether it's working. The scores are research-based judgements, so treat close scores as ties.

concepts.name: Leaflings
concepts.hook: Pick a photo of anything flat (a leaf, a petal, a ticket stub, a crisp). It becomes a little guy.
concepts.oneLiner: Choose a photo of a real flat object and its exact silhouette and colours become a wobbly critter with ink eyes and twig legs, who moves into your herbarium page and fills a field guide of about 30 shape classes.
concepts.pitch: Everyone has a pocket full of little flat things: the maple leaf from the walk home, a cinema ticket, a pressed petal, one perfectly curled crisp. Leaflings turns any of them into a shape-true critter in seconds. You pick a photo from your camera roll (or take one through the phone's own photo sheet), the object peels off the picture, blinks, grows legs and waddles onto a hand-drawn herbarium page. Shapes sort into a field guide of about 30 silhouette classes (maple, ginkgo, heart, needle, ticket, crisp...) with a 6 + 1 secret per season, villagers post a gentle request each morning ('the baker wants something red and pointy'), and every critter can be sent to a friend by link or saved as a sticker. The photo never leaves the phone. No two players own the same creatures, because the creatures come from their own pockets and pavements.

look.short: A kraft-paper herbarium page · real leaves with inked eyes and twig legs
look.vibe: Imagine opening an old botany notebook on a rainy afternoon. Pressed leaves are taped to the cream pages with little handwritten labels, and then one of them blinks. Its edges lift off the paper, two ink-dot eyes open, matchstick legs unfold, and it toddles to the next page to say hello to a ticket stub with a top hat.
look.layout: Portrait phone screen. Top: a slim paper tab with today's villager request in handwriting ('The baker wants something red and pointy') next to the villager's little face, and a row of seasonal silhouettes showing 6 + 1 slots. Bottom third: a big round 'find' button shaped like a magnifying glass, with 'pick a photo' and 'draw one' as two smaller buttons beside it. When you pick a photo, the page dims, your picture appears like a print on the desk, a dotted line traces around the object, it peels off with a paper rustle, eyes pop open, legs unfold, and the new critter walks onto the page and its silhouette fills in the field guide.

concepts.name: If It Fits
concepts.niche: Soft-body physics puzzle · cats are liquid · daily room
concepts.hook: Cats are liquid. Prove it: pour this chonk into a teacup.
concepts.oneLiner: A no-fail soft-body puzzle where you nudge, tip and coax squishy cats into teacups, boxes, boots and sinks until every cat fits and sits, with a new room every morning.
concepts.pitch: 'Cats are liquid' and 'if it fits, I sits' are two of the internet's oldest cat jokes, and nobody has made the game that proves them. In If It Fits each room has a few soft-body cats and some deeply unsuitable containers. You nudge and tip them, and they glorp, ooze and loaf into place. Each breed flows differently (a kitten pours like water, a Persian like honey, a chonk like pudding, a sphynx wobbles like jelly), so breeds are both the puzzle variety and a 6 + 1 secret collection. A new room arrives every morning, generated from a shared prop library and checked by a solver so it always has a fair par, and a sandbox photo room lets players pour any cat into anything and post the result. When the last cat settles, the camera pans over the room as the purring builds. It's a physics clip that sells itself and a perfect portal game.

concepts.name: Lemon Ink
concepts.niche: Little gifts by link · secret notes · tactile reveal
concepts.hook: Send a secret note. They have to iron it to read it.
concepts.oneLiner: Write a short hidden note, add a music-box tune if you like, and send it as a link; your friend smooths out the crumpled paper with a warm iron until your words bloom in brown lemon ink.
concepts.pitch: Group chats are full of words and short on gestures. Lemon Ink is a little gift you send by link: write up to about 200 characters, pick an occasion (birthday, Valentine's, sorry, thank you, 'open when you're sad'), choose your paper and, if you like, a tune from a pre-punched music-box library. Your friend opens a crumpled, coffee-stained page and has to iron it flat; wrinkles hiss away and your handwriting slowly browns into view, then the little music box plays. They tap 'write back', and the reply arrives stacked on top of yours. Every note you receive goes into a keepsake drawer. As you collect stationery, the reveal changes: hold a candle under it, rub a pencil across it, steam it over a kettle. It merges three gift ideas (Lemon Ink, Music Box Mail and Songbird) into one 'little gifts by link' brand, needs no server, and keeps the note in the link, with firm safeguards against misuse.

concepts.name: Cuttings
concepts.niche: Houseplant care · gift-by-link · living family trees
concepts.hook: This plant has lived in 4,000 phones. Here's your cutting. Grow it, snip it, pass it on.
concepts.oneLiner: A cozy houseplant game where new plants only arrive as cuttings sent by link, rare mutations appear only in descendants, and every plant carries a family tree back to a public mother plant named in a creator video.
concepts.pitch: Grow a Garden proved that gardening plus rare mutations is the biggest cozy fantasy going, and real plant people already make friends by handing out pothos cuttings in jam jars. Cuttings makes that ritual the whole game: you can't buy or find a plant, only receive one. Every newcomer gets a free cutting from a public mother plant (each creator video names one, like 'Biscuit'), so a stranger from TikTok is growing in seconds and joins one giant visible lineage. Tend it for a minute, snip a cutting when a node is ready, and send it by link. Rare traits (variegated, pink stem, heart leaf, moon leaf...) only ever show up in descendants, so the best plants are always gifts. Per-lineage leaderboards ('Biscuit: generation 31, 12 countries') give group chats something to race on, and milestone reveals ('your cutting now has 100 descendants') are the clip. Plants are drawn by an L-system from about eight hand-drawn leaf shapes, and a light server keeps every plant safe even when iOS wipes browser storage.

concepts.name: Fold Together
concepts.niche: Couch co-op · cloth physics · laundry folding for two
concepts.hook: Fold a fitted sheet with your partner. One phone, four thumbs. Try not to bicker.
concepts.oneLiner: A two-player cloth-physics game where each person holds two corners of a floppy sheet, on one phone or on two phones by link, folding a daily basket of three items (one of them absurd) and learning hotel folds that end in towel animals.
concepts.pitch: Every couple has fought over a fitted sheet, and 'cozy games for couples' is one of the most requested and least supplied lanes in the research. Fold Together turns that tiny domestic moment into a calm, untimed co-op toy: each person grabs two corners, you stretch, line up the edges and the cloth snaps into a crisp fold with a soft thwump. There are no fail states, only gentle bickering ('your other left'). A daily basket of three items (one absurd: an octopus costume, a parachute) ends in a shareable fold-score card, a hotel-fold path ends in towel animals (swan, elephant, cat), and your linen closet fills with neat stacks. Play on one phone laid flat between you, on two phones paired by link (for long-distance couples and friends), or as a Discord Activity inside a voice call. Fabrics are scans of real textiles, so the art is human-made by definition.

concepts.pitch: The islands have slipped beneath a gentle sea. concepts.oneLiner: A tiny window-box garden that grows along the bottom of your screen while you work, and your friends' plants can visit.
concepts.pitch: A small studio launchpad. Desktop idle games spread fast (Rusty's Retirement sold 330k+ copies on Steam at $7; Bongo Cat peaked at 194k concurrent players). Sill is a window box that sits at the bottom of the screen, grows while you work, and lets friends' plants pollinate yours. The goal is cash flow, Steam followers and a mailing list to launch the flagship to, not a fortune.
